walkthroughs.body_html:
Animal Physiology — a core area of Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Animal Physiology brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Animal Physiology.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Burnet's clonal selection theory of immunity dates from:

options: Inserting aquaporins in collecting duct
Closing aquaporins
Increasing glomerular filtration
Stimulating renin

mcqs.q: After pre-mRNA splicing in eukaryotes, which sequences remain in the mature mRNA?
options: Exons remain; introns are removed.
Introns remain because they encode the protein; exons are removed as junk.
Only Na+ moves during an action potential; K+ stays still.
Both introns and exons are removed and the cell uses just the cap and tail.

mcqs.q: During an action potential, do Na+ and K+ move through the same channels?
options: ADH directly opens holes in the collecting duct that let urine escape.
No — voltage-gated Na+ channels open first (depolarisation, Na+ in), then voltage-gated K+ channels open (repolarisation, K+ out).
Only Na+ moves during an action potential; K+ stays still.
Na+ and K+ swap places through the same channel at the same time.

mcqs.q: How does ADH affect the collecting duct in the kidney?
options: Only Na+ moves during an action potential; K+ stays still.
ADH actively pumps water out of urine into the blood.
It increases the permeability of the collecting duct to water (by inserting aquaporins), so more water is reabsorbed and urine is more concentrated.
ADH directly opens holes in the collecting duct that let urine escape.
